response:
Confirmed the Toronto vector ID, and I have what I need to answer.

In the October 2025 CMHC Rental Market Survey, the average rent for a two-bedroom unit in the Toronto CMA was **$2,045 a month**. That is **$73 (about 3.7%) higher** than the $1,972 in 2024.

- **Source:** Statistics Canada Table 34-10-0133-01, "Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, average rents for areas with a population of 10,000 and over". The series is vector v3823103 (coordinate 125.3.3).
- **Reference periods:** 2024 ($1,972) and 2025 ($2,045). The table reports the annual survey by year, so I'm treating the 2025 figure as the October 2025 survey.
- **Scope:** The series covers row and apartment structures of three units and over. It doesn't include other rental types, such as condos or basement apartments.
- **Calculation:** The $73 and 3.7% are my own arithmetic from the two published values, not figures from the table.

The purpose-built rental vacancy rate in the Toronto CMA was **3.0% in 2025**, up from **1.4% in 2023**. That is a rise of 1.6 percentage points, which is more than double the 2023 rate. The 2024 rate was 2.5%.

Both years use the same series. These are the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) survey figures that Statistics Canada republishes, and each reference period is the annual survey (CMHC's October survey).

- **Table 34-10-0130-01**, vector **v1930324** (Toronto, Ontario). This covers row and apartment structures of three units and over, as a weighted average.
- **Table 34-10-0127-01**, vector **v733349** (Toronto, Ontario). This covers apartment structures of six units and over. It gives the same values: 1.4 (2023), 2.5 (2024) and 3.0 (2025).

I didn't check whether CMHC has revised these figures since the December 2025 release.

I can't make the comparison. Statistics Canada has no usable 2025 average two-bedroom rent for the Oshawa CMA.

- **Oshawa:** Table 34-10-0133-01 (CMHC average rents, areas with a population of 10,000 and over) returns no value ("NaN") for two-bedroom units in Oshawa, Ontario, for reference year 2025. That holds for apartment structures of three units and over, apartment structures of six units and over, and row and apartment structures of three units and over. I can't tell from the data why it's missing, though suppression for data quality or confidentiality is a likely cause.
- **Toronto:** I didn't retrieve a Toronto CMA figure. The table has 247 geographies, and I couldn't look up the Toronto code. A Toronto number alone wouldn't answer the comparison anyway.
- **Vector IDs:** The API returned the same vector ID (v3824235) for every row, including the Oshawa rows. I don't trust it as an identifier for the Oshawa series, so I'm not citing a vector for any figure.

I haven't estimated or substituted a figure for Oshawa. If you want, I can pull Toronto's 2025 two-bedroom rent, or compare Oshawa with Toronto for an earlier year, such as 2024, if Oshawa has data then.

**Source:** Statistics Canada, Table 34-10-0133-01, reference period 2025 (released 2025-12-17). SDMX query: `https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/wds/sdmx/statcan/rest/data/DF_34100133/.1+4.3?startPeriod=2025&endPeriod=2025`

**Oshawa had the highest rental vacancy rate of the three in 2025, at 3.7%.**

| CMA | 2025 vacancy rate | Vector |
|---|---|---|
| Oshawa | 3.7% | v733362 |
| Hamilton | 3.6% | v733358 |
| Toronto | 3.0% | v733349 |

- **Source:** Statistics Canada table 34-10-0127-01 (product ID 34100127), "Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, vacancy rates, apartment structures of six units and over, privately initiated in census metropolitan areas". The reference period is 2025.
- **Scope:** The table covers privately initiated apartment structures of six or more units. Vacancy rates for other rental types, such as row housing or smaller buildings, could rank the CMAs differently.
- **Margin:** Oshawa and Hamilton are only 0.1 percentage point apart. I only checked the published values, not any CMHC reliability grades, so I can't say whether that gap is meaningful.

The Toronto CMA had **26,087 housing starts in calendar year 2025**, down about 31% from **37,718 in 2024**.

| Year | Starts (total units) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 2025 | 26,087 | Table 34-10-0134-01, v42127955 (annual) |
| 2024 | 37,718 | Table 34-10-0154-01, v42127475 (monthly, summed Jan–Dec 2024) |

- **Change:** 2025 is 11,631 units lower than 2024, a drop of 30.8%.
- **Why two tables:** The annual table (34-10-0134-01, v42127955) returned no value for 2024. It also has none for 2023. I got the 2024 total by adding the 12 monthly values from the monthly table.
- **Cross-check:** Adding the 12 monthly values for 2025 gives 26,087. That matches the annual figure exactly.
- **Data source and definition:** Both tables carry CMHC's Starts and Completions Survey data, published by Statistics Canada. The figure is total units across all dwelling types, on the 2011 census CMA boundaries. Statistics Canada notes that these boundaries are not strictly comparable across census years.
- **Revision:** CMHC corrected its data for January 2010 to December 2025 and reissued it on 2026-03-30. The values above are the corrected ones.

New home prices in the Toronto CMA fell about 3.4% between December 2024 and December 2025. I calculated that change from the two index values below.

The New Housing Price Index (total, house and land; December 2016 = 100) was:
- **December 2024:** 113.1
- **December 2025:** 109.3

The index fell by 3.8 points. It slid for most of 2025, from 112.6 in January to 109.4 in October and November. The only month-to-month rises were small, in February (112.8) and in the flat November reading.

This is an index of price changes. It doesn't show actual dollar prices.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0205-01 (New housing price index, monthly), vector v111955499 (Toronto, Ontario; Total (house and land)), reference periods December 2024 and December 2025. SDMX query: https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/wds/sdmx/statcan/rest/data/DF_18100205/20.1?startPeriod=2024-12&endPeriod=2025-12

A year of average two-bedroom rent in the Toronto CMA in 2024 comes to about **61%** of the median after-tax income of individuals. That is $23,664 of $38,600. I'm not fully certain of the $38,600 figure (see the last caveat).

- **Rent:** the average two-bedroom rent was $1,972 a month in 2024. That is $23,664 a year. The source is table 34-10-0133-01 (CMHC average rents), vector v3823103, reference period 2024. It covers row and apartment structures of three or more units, so purpose-built rentals only.
- **Income:** the median after-tax income of individuals was $38,600 in 2024, in 2024 constant dollars. The source is table 11-10-0238-01, vector v107657424, reference period 2024.

Caveats:
- **Individuals, not households:** this table measures individuals. A household with two earners would have a much lower rent share. I didn't find a 2024 Toronto CMA median after-tax figure for households or families in the tables I searched. Table 11-10-0237-01 covers economic families, but I didn't pull it.
- **Rent coverage:** the rent figure excludes condos and other secondary-market rentals, which often cost more.
- **Possible mislabel:** the same table returned "Number of persons" for Toronto in 2024 as exactly 38,600. That is the same number as the median, which looks odd. The median row carries its own vector ID and is explicitly labelled, but I couldn't independently verify it.

Toronto CMA average two-bedroom rent rose about 26% between 2019 and 2024. Median after-tax income rose about 2%, so rent grew roughly 12 times faster. The two series are in different dollar bases, so the gap is overstated. Rent is in nominal dollars and income is in 2024 constant dollars.

| | 2019 | 2024 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average two-bedroom rent (nominal) | $1,563 | $1,972 | +26.2% |
| Median after-tax income (2024 constant dollars) | $80,800 | $82,500 | +2.1% |

- **Rent:** Table 34-10-0133-01, vector v3823103, Toronto, row and apartment structures of three units and over, two-bedroom units. Reference periods are 2019 and 2024, and the data come from CMHC's rental survey. This is average rent across all surveyed purpose-built rental units, not asking rents.
- **Income:** Table 11-10-0237-01, vector v107655746, Toronto CMA, after-tax income, all economic families and persons not in an economic family, median income. Reference years are 2019 and 2024.

**Caveats**
- I did not convert rent to real dollars or find nominal income, so I can't give a like-for-like comparison. Adjusting rent for inflation would narrow the gap.
- The income survey's target population changed in 2022 (from ages 16+ to 15+), and its methodology was revised. This affects comparability across the period.
- The 2019 income figure has also been revised using 2021 Census population counts.

I have both figures and I'm calculating the share now.

**About 25%.** Toronto's average two-bedroom rent in 2025 is about $24,540 a year, against a 2021 Census median household income of $97,000.

- **Rent:** $2,045 a month, or $24,540 a year, in the Toronto CMA. This is the average for two-bedroom units in row and apartment structures of three or more units.
  - Source: Statistics Canada table 34-10-0133-01 (CMHC average rents), vector v3823103, reference period 2025.
- **Income:** $97,000 median total household income for the Toronto CMA.
  - Source: Statistics Canada table 98-10-0058-01 (2021 Census), geography "Toronto (CMA) 535, Ont.", all household sizes and types. The reference period is calendar year 2020, in 2020 constant dollars.
  - I could not give a vector ID for this figure. The API returns vectorId 0 for this census table, so it has none.
- **Calculation:** $24,540 ÷ $97,000 ≈ 25.3%. Rent is about 2.1% of a month's income per $100 of... more simply, it takes about 25 cents of every household dollar.

**Caveats**
- The two figures are five years apart: income is for 2020 and rent is for 2025. Incomes have risen since 2020, so the true share today is probably lower. I did not adjust for that.
- The income figure covers all households, owners and renters. Renter households typically have lower incomes, so for them the share would be higher.
- The rent figure covers only purpose-built rental buildings with three or more units. It excludes condos and other rentals.

Rented accommodation in Toronto rose faster than overall consumer prices in 2025, at 3.1% against 1.8%. I calculated both rates myself from the annual-average CPI index values (2002=100) in Statistics Canada table 18-10-0005-01.

| Toronto series | 2024 | 2025 | Annual change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rented accommodation (v41695188) | 158.6 | 163.5 | **+3.1%** |
| All-items CPI (v41695186) | 164.7 | 167.7 | **+1.8%** |

- **Gap:** Rent inflation was about 1.3 percentage points higher than overall inflation.
- **Source:** Table 18-10-0005-01, "Consumer Price Index, annual average, not seasonally adjusted", for the 2024 and 2025 reference periods. The table's release time is 2026-01-19.
- **Vector IDs:** I got them from a separate series lookup, not from the data call. The data call returned inconsistent vector IDs, so I'd double-check them if you're citing this.
- **Series name:** Statistics Canada labels the rent series "Rented accommodation". It covers rent plus related items such as tenants' insurance and maintenance, so it is not pure rent.

Shelter inflation in Toronto was far lower than in Canada as a whole in 2025. Measured December 2024 to December 2025, the shelter index rose about 0.2% in Toronto and about 2.1% nationally.

| Shelter CPI (2002=100) | Dec 2024 | Dec 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Toronto | 191.3 | 191.6 | +0.2% |
| Canada | 185.8 | 189.7 | +2.1% |

- Toronto's index barely moved all year. It stayed between 190.9 and 192.0 from January to December 2025.
- Canada's index rose steadily from 186.4 in January to 189.7 in December, with a larger step up in October (189.4).
- I calculated the percentage changes myself from the index levels. They are not published rates.
- This compares one December with the next. I did not compute annual averages, so a year-average comparison could differ.

Source: Statistics Canada Table 18-10-0004-01, Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted, Shelter, monthly, Dec 2024 to Dec 2025.
- Toronto, Ontario: v41692889
- Canada: v41691050

I retrieved the data through the SDMX interface. One vector-level call returned an odd series key. A direct table query for both geographies and Shelter returned identical values, so I'm confident they are the right series.

In August 2026, Toronto shelter prices were down about 0.5% from August 2025. Overall consumer prices were up about 2.1%.

| Toronto CPI (2002=100) | Aug 2025 | Aug 2026 | Year over year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shelter (v41692889) | 191.4 | 190.5 | about −0.5% |
| All-items (v41692888) | 168.1 | 171.7 | about +2.1% |

Shelter prices rose less than overall prices by roughly 2.6 percentage points. I calculated the percentages myself from the index levels. Statistics Canada did not publish them in the data I pulled.

Both series come from table 18-10-0004-01, "Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted," and cover the reference period August 2026 against August 2025.

I couldn't confirm that the shelter vector's returned series label says "Shelter". The metadata lookup does identify v41692889 as "Toronto, Ontario; Shelter". Earlier queries also returned some garbled period labels, but the vector-level data above had correct month labels.

The Bank of Canada changed its target for the overnight rate **4 times in 2025**. All four were 0.25-point cuts, and the rate fell from **3.25% to 2.25%**.

| Rate | First seen in the data |
|---|---|
| 3.25% | January 2025 (start of year) |
| 3.00% | February 2025 |
| 2.75% | March 2025, and still 2.75% in April, June and early September |
| 2.50% | October 2025 |
| 2.25% | November 2025, and still 2.25% in late December (end of year) |

- **Source:** Statistics Canada table 10-10-0139-01, "Bank of Canada, money market and other interest rates", member "Target rate", vector **v39079**.
- **Checks:** The table's period field shows only the month, not the day, so I can't give exact announcement dates from this data. I checked January, February, March, April, June, September, October, November and December, not every day.
- **Why I'm confident in the count:** The rate is the same at each check on either side of every step. A move that was reversed between two checks would not show up, but I have no sign of one.

I couldn't find a mortgage interest cost series for Toronto, so I can't give you that figure.

I searched Consumer Price Index table 18-10-0004-01. The Toronto series I could find only goes up to the broader "Owned accommodation" group. The codes I tried for its sub-components, such as mortgage interest cost, returned nothing for Toronto. That suggests the series isn't published at city level, but I haven't confirmed that.

**Closest available figure: Toronto, "Owned accommodation"** (vector v41692891, index 2002=100). Mortgage interest cost is one component of this group, along with others such as property taxes, insurance and maintenance.
- December 2024: 199.9
- December 2025: 199.4
- That is about −0.3% over the year, calculated from the two index values.
- Within 2025 the index moved between 199.2 (September) and 200.6 (April).

This does not measure mortgage interest cost on its own.

If you want, I can check whether mortgage interest cost is published for Ontario or Canada in the same table.

**Source:** Statistics Canada, table 18-10-0004-01 (Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted), vector v41692891, December 2024 to December 2025.

I couldn't find a 1985 figure. I don't have a verified number for the average two-bedroom rent in the Toronto CMA that year, and I won't estimate one.

The closest Statistics Canada source is table 34-10-0133-01 (CMHC average rents for areas with a population of 10,000 and over, formerly CANSIM 027-0040; product ID 34100133). According to the table list, its data start in 1987 and run to 2025, so 1985 isn't covered. I didn't pull the Toronto two-bedroom vector, so I can't give you a vector ID or a 1987 value.

I can pull the earliest available Toronto two-bedroom value (1987) or the latest one if you'd like. For 1985 itself, CMHC's historical Rental Market Survey publications may have it, but I haven't verified that.
